big: Same ₹1 lakh, three funds. One holds mostly shares, one mostly bonds, one a mix. They will not behave alike, and that is the whole point of choosing well.

lines: So which type should I pick? My colleague says equity, my father says debt.
Both are partly right. It depends on when you need the money. Let us first see what each kind actually holds.

alt: Bars showing a typical mix of shares and bonds in equity, hybrid and debt funds
caps: An equity fund keeps most of its money in company shares.
A hybrid fund mixes shares and bonds in one fund.
A debt fund keeps most of its money in bonds.
These are typical mixes. Each fund's own paper tells you the real split.

intro: These are built a little differently from the three above.
rows: Copies an index such as the Nifty 50, no manager picking stocks
An equity fund with a 3-year lock-in, for the old tax regime deduction
note: Under the old tax regime, up to ₹1.5 lakh a year in an ELSS can be claimed as a deduction. Check the current rules before you decide.

q: Meena needs ₹3 lakh for a wedding in 18 months. Which choice best fits the goal?
opts: An equity fund, since shares always beat bonds over any period of time
An ELSS, since the lock-in keeps the money safe from market falls
A fund chosen only for the highest return in the last year
A steadier fund, since a fall could hit just when the money is needed
why: Shares can fall for long stretches. Over 18 months there is no guarantee they will beat bonds.
A lock-in stops withdrawals. It does not stop the value from falling, and it is longer than 18 months.
Last year's return says little about the next 18 months and ignores the risk behind it.
With under two years to go, a steadier fund limits the chance of a fall just before the wedding.

q: Rohan is 28 and invests for retirement in 30 years. A friend says: 'Put it all in a debt fund, it is safer.' What is the best reply?
opts: Agree, because safer is always better whatever the time frame may be
With 30 years ahead, equity's swings can even out; debt alone may lag
Agree, since debt funds cannot lose value in any single year at all
Disagree, because debt funds are not allowed for retirement goals
why: Safer in a short span is not safer in 30 years. Slow growth can lose to rising prices.
A long horizon gives equity time to recover from falls, while a debt-only mix may not keep up with prices.
Debt funds can lose value, for example when interest rates rise or a borrower fails to pay.
No rule bans debt funds for retirement. They are simply a poor sole choice for a long horizon.

q: An index fund and an actively managed equity fund both hold large companies. What is the main difference?
opts: The index fund copies a set list; the active fund's manager picks holdings
The index fund holds bonds, while the active fund holds shares
The index fund is guaranteed to match the best fund, while the active fund is not
The index fund cannot fall when the market falls, since it only tracks it
why: The index fund copies a published list. The active fund's manager decides what to buy and sell.
Both hold shares here. What differs is who decides the holdings, not the asset type.
An index fund matches its index, not the best fund, and active funds sometimes do better.
An index fund falls with its index. Tracking it means following it down as well as up.

q: A colleague claims an ELSS is the safest equity fund because of its three-year lock-in. What is the flaw?
opts: There is no flaw, because the lock-in protects the invested amount from loss
ELSS funds hold bonds, which protect against falls during the lock-in
The lock-in only stops selling, so the value can still fall in the three years
The lock-in ends when markets fall, so the money is released for you
why: The lock-in restricts selling. It does not shield the value from changes in the market.
An ELSS is an equity fund holding mostly shares, not bonds.
A lock-in limits when you can sell. The fund still holds shares, whose prices can fall.
The lock-in does not end when markets fall. The three years apply to each instalment.

pts: Equity grows more and swings more. Debt is steadier, but not without risk.
Hybrid mixes the two. An index fund copies an index. An ELSS is equity with a 3-year lock-in.
Pick by goal and time frame: soon needs steady, far away can handle swings.
